Vantage 1 vs Vantage 2. Which is better?

Vantage 1 pros: Farther beam distance, longer battery life (6hours), does not require allen key to tighten.

Vantage 2: Lighter than vantage 1 but not a whole lot, noticeably smaller but because of the size it can only accommodate 1 battery and therefore has a shorter battery life (2.25hours). Much cheaper than Vantage 1

The big difference between the two is the beam pattern.
Vantage 1 is more of a thrower with a focused beam that can reach long distances. While Vantage 2 has a wider spot than the Vantage 1 but less throwing power.

Ideally a focused beam is best in smokey situations and not a flood light. Do note that Vantage 2 is not a flood light, it just has more flood than the Vantage 1. See pictures for comparison

When buying flashlights, it is important to not get focused on the lumen output alone but also the candela rating. 
A throw(spot) light will generally have a much lower lumen output but higher candela rating. While a flood light will have more lumen output but less candela rating.

TL;DR 
No, the Vantage 2 does not make Vantage 1 obsolete. It is a different light, otherwise Streamlight would have discontinued it already.
Both are equally good helmet mounted lights and it all comes down to preference or budget which we hope this post helped you in a way.

Here's why Halloween celebrants bedeck their homes in these contrasting colours.
By Meghan Jones

We tend to take special holiday colours for granted, not giving them too much thought since they’re so ingrained in our culture. Despite Halloween looking pretty different this year, the colours are pretty consistent. It’s usually pretty obvious what colours go with which celebratory days – all you need to do is step into most general or supermarkets to see full aisles inundated with the hues of the season. But what might be less obvious is why certain colours are associated with certain holidays. Why are Christmas colours red and green, for instance? Of course, sometimes the colours are self-explanatory: the association of green with St. Patrick’s Day, for instance. But other times, the colours can seem random.

For instance, as black and orange begin to take over supermarket aisles and pop up outside homes as decorations, we wonder how these colours became so popular for Halloween. Is it just because of black cats and pumpkins, or is there a deeper meaning to it?

Black

In the early days of Halloween-like celebrations, black actually was supposed to be more sad than spooky. To learn how these colours became associated with Halloween, we’ll have to explore the history of the holiday itself. Halloween can trace its origins back to a pagan celebration called Samhain, a ritual that the ancient Celts celebrated in late October and early November. This is because it was approximately halfway between the fall equinox and winter solstice. The purpose of the celebration was to welcome in the time of harvest, and with it, “the dark half of the year,” according to History.com. So, there’s some darkness already.

But the true symbolic significance of black had to do with death, as did the holiday. The ancient Celts believed that during Samhain, the boundaries between the living and the dead were weakened. So the celebration would also include tributes and offerings to deceased ancestors, and celebrants wore deep black mourning dress.

Orange

Orange is a little more self-explanatory. But it also has to do with the particular time of year for the northern hemisphere. Again, Samhain was ushering in the harvest time; people would have seen the trees turn orange after months of greenery. But the orange also has to do with another important component of the ancient Samhain celebrations: fire. The ancient Celts would light community fires while leaving the fires in their own hearths to burn out. The fires could also be rituals to help ward off evil spirits while the gateway between the living and the dead was weak. And those fires certainly would have been orange!

Today, our Halloween traditions range from sinister to cheerful and everything in between.
